props.title: Keeping the Faith
props.initialSlug: A priest and a rabbi both fall for the same woman

sections.content: Keeping the Faith (2000) marks Edward Norton's directorial debut, tackling interfaith romance with surprising nuance and wit. This romantic comedy uniquely centers on a Catholic priest (Norton) and a Rabbi (Ben Stiller) who both fall for their childhood friend Anna (Jenna Elfman). It follows in the tradition of religion-themed comedies like Sister Act (1992) and Nuns on the Run (1990), but brings a fresh perspective by treating faith seriously while maintaining genuine humor. The film stands out for refusing to mock its religious characters while still finding comedy in their situations.

sections.content: Norton's direction shows remarkable sensitivity in handling both religious tradition and modern romance. Like The Jazz Singer (1927) and Fiddler on the Roof (1971), the film explores how religious leaders balance tradition with changing times. The chemistry between Norton, Stiller, and Elfman drives the story, while supporting performances from Anne Bancroft and Milos Forman add gravitas to scenes dealing with faith and community expectations.

What sets Keeping the Faith apart is its authentic portrayal of religious life in contemporary New York City. Unlike broader religious comedies like Bruce Almighty (2003), it depicts the day-to-day reality of religious leadership while exploring universal themes of friendship, love, and duty. The film's handling of interfaith relationships predates later explorations like Meet the Fockers (2004) and offers a more nuanced take on religious identity in modern America. SUBHEAD: Balancing Comedy and Faith

The film succeeds by finding humor in human nature rather than religious mockery. While films like Life of Brian (1979) derive comedy from religious satire, Keeping the Faith finds its laughs in the universal experiences of friendship and romance. Norton's direction maintains this delicate balance, allowing the characters' faith to inform their choices without becoming caricatures.
